title: Evidence of Pinniped Depredation Activity in South Georgia's Patagonian Toothfish Fishery
content:
ABSTRACT

Marine mammal depredation is an important consideration within sustainable management. Studies on depredation activity in South Georgia's Patagonian toothfish (Dissostichus eleginoides) fishery have focused on odontocetes, with little attention directed toward pinnipeds. This study provides the first detailed description of fishery-leopard seal (Hydrurga leptonyx) interactions and explores multiyear spatial and temporal trends in the depredation behavior of both leopard seals and Antarctic fur seals (Arctocephalus gazella) in the toothfish fishery. Although less frequent than odontocete depredation, pinnipeds repeatedly depredated the Patagonian toothfish longline fishery. The likelihood of pinniped depredation increased through the fishing season (April–August) and differed between continental shelves in both species. Interannual variation in depredation rates was apparent, with no recorded depredation events post-2021, coinciding with a fleet-wide alteration in the hauling configuration of the fishing vessels. It remains unclear whether the updated configuration prevents depredation activity or obstructs observers' ability to accurately record this behavior. Based on the limitations of the current data, we outline recommendations to enhance the data-collection process, which will support future investigations into the drivers of this behavior and potential mitigation measures. Addressing these knowledge gaps will guide effective sustainable fisheries management and reduce fisheries–wildlife conflict.
